title: Rate limits are charged at whichever point in the call the true amount becomes knowable
content:
The chunk is explicit and unusually self-aware about *when* a rate limit is decreased. A...8.1.5 decreases `LIMIT_CURVE_SWAP` "before the exchange is executed" and A...8.2.5 decreases `LIMIT_CURVE_DEPOSIT` "before liquidity is added" — both from caller-supplied inputs that are already known. Conversely A...7.2.4 notes that `withdrawAave` "is rate limited at the end of the function rather than before", using the decoded `amountWithdrawn`; A...8.3.6 likewise charges `LIMIT_CURVE_WITHDRAW` from the actually withdrawn tokens "after liquidity is removed"; and A...9.1.7 charges the Uniswap swap limit by `startingBalance - endingBalance`.

The organising rule is information availability. Where the debited quantity is an input, charge before and get pre-authorisation semantics. Where the quantity is only produced by the external protocol, charge after and get accuracy.

The trade-off is real in the post-hoc cases: the external interaction has already happened by the time the limit is consulted, so a rate limit can be *overdrawn* in the sense that the breach is detected only as the decrease reverts — which then reverts the whole transaction. Atomicity is doing the work that ordering does in the pre-charge cases.

The deeper point is that a rate limit charged against a requested amount and one charged against a realised amount are different controls. Grove uses both, deliberately, and the Atlas records which is which per function rather than leaving it to implementation habit.
description: Curve swaps and deposits debit up front from known inputs; withdrawAave and removeLiquidityCurve debit at the end from returned amounts — accuracy is preferred over pre-authorisation.
